items.stem: Which of the following best describes "vector"?
options: Negative acceleration – a decrease in velocity per unit time
The distance travelled per unit time (a scalar)
Finding the area of a region with straight sloping top as ½ × (sum of parallel sides) × width
A quantity that has both magnitude and direction, e.g. displacement, velocity, force, acceleration
items.answer: A quantity that has both magnitude and direction, e.g. displacement, velocity, force, acceleration
items.markingKey: D. "vector" is a quantity that has both magnitude and direction, e.g. displacement, velocity, force, acceleration.

items.stem: Explain why a distance–time graph for an object moving at constant speed is a straight line.
items.answer: Equal distances are covered in equal times, so distance increases by the same amount each second and the gradient (speed) is constant.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Equal distances are covered in equal times, so distance increases by the same amount each second and the gradient (speed) is constant. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between velocity and speed.
items.answer: Speed is distance per unit time (scalar); velocity is displacement per unit time in a stated direction (vector).
items.markingKey: Speed is distance per unit time (scalar); velocity is displacement per unit time in a stated direction (vector). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Amara writes: "Two cars travelling at 60 km/h have the same velocity." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: They only have the same velocity if they move in the same direction; speed is the same but velocity may differ.
items.markingKey: They only have the same velocity if they move in the same direction; speed is the same but velocity may differ. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Kenji is investigating how the height of a ramp affects the average speed of a toy car rolling 1.0 m down it. Formulate a testable hypothesis and justify it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: If the ramp height increases, then the average speed will increase, because more gravitational potential energy is transferred to kinetic energy.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: testable prediction in "if … then …" form linking the independent and dependent variables; 1-2 marks: scientific explanation. Model: If the ramp height increases, then the average speed will increase, because more gravitational potential energy is transferred to kinetic energy.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that average speed cameras are fairer than fixed speed cameras.
items.answer: Average speed cameras measure what matters (speed over distance) and are fairer, though privacy and cost must be managed.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: measure behaviour over a long stretch, not just at one point; drivers cannot simply brake at the camera; smoother traffic flow. Arguments against: expensive to install; privacy concerns from number-plate tracking; drivers may watch speedometer instead of road. Supported judgement: Average speed cameras measure what matters (speed over distance) and are fairer, though privacy and cost must be managed.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "scalar".
items.answer: A quantity that has magnitude (size) only, e.g. distance, speed, mass, time
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a quantity that has magnitude (size) only, e.g. distance, speed, mass, time. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between displacement and distance.
items.answer: Distance is the total length of the path (scalar); displacement is the straight-line separation from start to finish with a direction (vector).
items.markingKey: Distance is the total length of the path (scalar); displacement is the straight-line separation from start to finish with a direction (vector). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims that two cars travelling at 60 km/h have the same velocity. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: They only have the same velocity if they move in the same direction; speed is the same but velocity may differ.
items.markingKey: They only have the same velocity if they move in the same direction; speed is the same but velocity may differ. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Arjun used light gates to measure the time for a trolley to travel 1.00 m down ramps of different heights.

Ramp height / cm | Time to travel 1.00 m / s: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
5 | 2.55 | 2.55 | 2.62
10 | 1.84 | 1.74 | 1.83
15 | 1.40 | 1.46 | 1.44
20 | 1.22 | 1.22 | 1.26
25 | 1.16 | 1.14 | 1.13

Calculate the mean time to travel 1.00 m when the ramp height was 10 cm.
items.markingKey: M1 (1.84 + 1.74 + 1.83) ÷ 3; A1 1.80 s (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: "A negative velocity means the object is slowing down." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: A negative velocity means motion in the opposite direction to the one chosen as positive.
items.markingKey: A negative velocity means motion in the opposite direction to the one chosen as positive. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A plane flies 600 km north and then 800 km east in a total time of 2.5 h. (a) Calculate the total distance and the displacement (magnitude and bearing). (b) Calculate the average speed and the average velocity. (c) Explain why the two answers to (b) are different.
items.answer: (a) distance 1400 km; displacement √(600² + 800²) = 1000 km on a bearing of 053°. (b) average speed 560 km/h; average velocity 400 km/h on bearing 053°. (c) Speed uses total path length (scalar); velocity uses straight-line displacement with a direction (vector).
items.markingKey: (a) distance 1400 km; displacement √(600² + 800²) = 1000 km on a bearing of 053°. (b) average speed 560 km/h; average velocity 400 km/h on bearing 053°. (c) Speed uses total path length (scalar); velocity uses straight-line displacement with a direction (vector).

items.stem: Approximately what is the acceleration of an object in free fall near the Earth’s surface?
items.answer: 9.8 m/s²
items.markingKey: 9.8 m/s². g ≈ 9.8 m/s² (often 10).

items.stem: Explain the difference between a distance–time graph and a velocity–time graph.
items.answer: The gradient of a distance–time graph is speed; the gradient of a velocity–time graph is acceleration and its area is distance travelled.
items.markingKey: The gradient of a distance–time graph is speed; the gradient of a velocity–time graph is acceleration and its area is distance travelled. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims that a downward-sloping line on a velocity–time graph means the object is moving backwards. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It means the velocity is decreasing (decelerating); the object is still moving forwards while velocity is positive.
items.markingKey: It means the velocity is decreasing (decelerating); the object is still moving forwards while velocity is positive. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Amara released a trolley from rest on a slope and used a data logger to record its velocity at intervals.

Time / s | Velocity / m/s: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0.5 | 0.38 | 0.37 | 0.37
1.0 | 0.77 | 0.76 | 0.76
1.5 | 1.14 | 1.15 | 1.11
2.0 | 1.46 | 1.45 | 1.53
2.5 | 1.88 | 1.87 | 1.86

Calculate the mean velocity when the time was 2.5 s.
items.markingKey: M1 (1.88 + 1.87 + 1.86) ÷ 3; A1 1.87 m/s (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: Using Usain Bolt’s 100 m world record (Berlin, 2009) as an example, explain acceleration and velocity–time graphs.
items.answer: He reached about 12 m/s within about 4 s of the start and finished in 9.58 s. His velocity–time graph rises steeply at first (large acceleration) then levels off near top speed (zero acceleration).
items.markingKey: Context (He reached about 12 m/s within about 4 s of the start and finished in 9.58 s.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: His velocity–time graph rises steeply at first (large acceleration) then levels off near top speed (zero acceleration). – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to acceleration and velocity–time graphs.

items.stem: Chloé writes: "An object with a large velocity must have a large acceleration." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A plane cruising at 250 m/s at constant velocity has zero acceleration; acceleration depends on change in velocity.
items.markingKey: A plane cruising at 250 m/s at constant velocity has zero acceleration; acceleration depends on change in velocity. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A lift starts from rest, accelerates uniformly at 1.5 m/s² for 2 s, travels at constant velocity for 6 s, then decelerates uniformly to rest in 3 s. (a) Calculate the maximum velocity. (b) Sketch the velocity–time graph with values. (c) Calculate the deceleration. (d) Calculate the total distance travelled.
items.answer: (a) v = 1.5 × 2 = 3 m/s (b) rise 0→3 m/s over 0–2 s, flat to 8 s, fall to 0 at 11 s (c) 3/3 = 1 m/s² (d) 3 + 18 + 4.5 = 25.5 m
items.markingKey: (a) v = 1.5 × 2 = 3 m/s (b) rise 0→3 m/s over 0–2 s, flat to 8 s, fall to 0 at 11 s (c) 3/3 = 1 m/s² (d) 3 + 18 + 4.5 = 25.5 m

items.stem: To what extent is it true that electric cars are safer than petrol cars because they accelerate faster?
items.answer: Faster acceleration is not in itself a safety advantage; safety depends on many design and behavioural factors.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: rapid acceleration helps when merging or overtaking; low centre of gravity from batteries reduces rollover. Arguments against: high acceleration can lead to loss of control by inexperienced drivers; heavier cars cause more damage in collisions; safety depends mostly on driver behaviour, braking and design. Supported judgement: Faster acceleration is not in itself a safety advantage; safety depends on many design and behavioural factors. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "deceleration"?
options: A quantity that has magnitude (size) only, e.g. distance, speed, mass, time
The mean of initial and final velocity, (u + v)/2
Negative acceleration – a decrease in velocity per unit time
Equal to the distance travelled (displacement) during that time
items.answer: Negative acceleration – a decrease in velocity per unit time
items.markingKey: C. "deceleration" is negative acceleration – a decrease in velocity per unit time.

items.stem: Explain why a negative gradient on a velocity–time graph means deceleration (if velocity is positive).
items.answer: Velocity is decreasing with time, so the change in velocity is negative and the acceleration is negative.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Velocity is decreasing with time, so the change in velocity is negative and the acceleration is negative. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between acceleration and velocity.
items.answer: Velocity is the rate of change of displacement (m/s); acceleration is the rate of change of velocity (m/s²).
items.markingKey: Velocity is the rate of change of displacement (m/s); acceleration is the rate of change of velocity (m/s²). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that velocity–time graphs from phone GPS apps give accurate distances for sports training.
items.answer: Good enough for general training but not accurate for sprints or precise measurements.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: convenient and automatic; area calculated by the app; good for long, steady runs. Arguments against: GPS errors of several metres, especially among tall buildings; sampling interval misses quick changes in speed; poor for short sprints. Supported judgement: Good enough for general training but not accurate for sprints or precise measurements.

items.answer: Displacement in the opposite direction

items.answer: Maya: triangle ½ × 6 × 12 = 36 m; Mateo: rectangle 11 × 6 = 66 m; Mateo travels further.
items.markingKey: 1 distance = area under v–t graph; 1 Maya 36 m and Mateo 66 m; 1 conclusion.

items.answer: When acceleration is constant

items.stem: Distinguish between v = u + at and v² = u² + 2as.
items.answer: v = u + at links velocity and time (no displacement); v² = u² + 2as links velocity and displacement (no time).
items.markingKey: v = u + at links velocity and time (no displacement); v² = u² + 2as links velocity and displacement (no time). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims that if a car doubles its speed, its braking distance doubles. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: From v² = u² + 2as, braking distance is proportional to u², so it quadruples.
items.markingKey: From v² = u² + 2as, braking distance is proportional to u², so it quadruples. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A pebble is dropped from rest down a well and hits the water after 2.5 s. Ignoring air resistance, how deep is the well? (g = 9.8 m/s²)

Near a school the speed limit is 20 m/s; on the main road it is 30 m/s. A driver has a reaction time of 1.0 s and the car decelerates at 6.5 m/s². (a) Calculate the stopping distance at each speed. (b) Show that the braking distance increases by a factor of 2.25 when the speed increases by a factor of 1.5. (c) Use your answers to justify low speed limits near schools.
items.answer: (a) 50.8 m and 99.2 m (b) braking ∝ u², (1.5)² = 2.25 (c) stopping distance is much shorter at low speed, so drivers can stop before hitting a child who steps out
items.markingKey: (a) M1 thinking = u × 1.0; M1 braking = u²/(2 × 6.5); A1 50.8 m; A1 99.2 m. (b) 1 from v² = u² + 2as, s ∝ u². (c) 1 reasoned link to safety/impact speed.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "free fall".
items.answer: Motion under gravity alone, with acceleration g ≈ 9.8 m/s² downwards (air resistance negligible)
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: motion under gravity alone, with acceleration g ≈ 9.8 m/s² downwards (air resistance negligible). Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why a ball dropped and a ball thrown horizontally from the same height (with no air resistance) hit the ground at the same time.
items.answer: Vertical motion is independent of horizontal motion; both start with zero vertical velocity and have the same vertical acceleration g, so s = ½gt² gives the same time.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Vertical motion is independent of horizontal motion; both start with zero vertical velocity and have the same vertical acceleration g, so s = ½gt² gives the same time. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Isabel dropped a ball from different heights and measured the time to fall with light gates.

Drop height / m | Fall time / s: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0.5 | 0.290 | 0.280 | 0.284
1.0 | 0.414 | 0.396 | 0.414
1.5 | 0.498 | 0.487 | 0.481
2.0 | 0.542 | 0.565 | 0.543
2.5 | 0.637 | 0.624 | 0.610

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: Fall time increases with height, but not proportionally – doubling the height increases the time by about 1.4 times (√2). For uniform acceleration from rest s = ½gt², so t = √(2s/g); time is proportional to the square root of height.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: Fall time increases with height, but not proportionally – doubling the height increases the time by about 1.4 times (√2).; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: For uniform acceleration from rest s = ½gt², so t = √(2s/g); time is proportional to the square root of height.

items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: Ana is investigating how accurately the area under a velocity–time graph (from a data-logger) predicts the measured distance travelled by a trolley. Identify the independent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: angle of the ramp (to give different accelerations)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: angle of the ramp (to give different accelerations) (the variable that is deliberately changed). The measured variable scores 0.

items.stem: "A ball thrown upwards has zero acceleration at the top of its flight." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Its velocity is zero at the top, but acceleration is still 9.8 m/s² downwards.
items.markingKey: Its velocity is zero at the top, but acceleration is still 9.8 m/s² downwards. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that electric cars are safer than petrol cars because they accelerate faster.
items.answer: Faster acceleration is not in itself a safety advantage; safety depends on many design and behavioural factors.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: rapid acceleration helps when merging or overtaking; low centre of gravity from batteries reduces rollover. Arguments against: high acceleration can lead to loss of control by inexperienced drivers; heavier cars cause more damage in collisions; safety depends mostly on driver behaviour, braking and design. Supported judgement: Faster acceleration is not in itself a safety advantage; safety depends on many design and behavioural factors.

items.stem: Hana investigated how the height of a ramp affects the average speed of a toy car rolling 1.0 m down it. The method had this weakness: time was measured with a hand-held stopwatch. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: use light gates (or video analysis) to remove reaction-time error of about 0.2 s
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: use light gates (or video analysis) to remove reaction-time error of about 0.2 s

items.stem: Mohammed plans an investigation into how accurately the area under a velocity–time graph (from a data-logger) predicts the measured distance travelled by a trolley. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (angle of the ramp (to give different accelerations)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: "Using g = 10 m/s² instead of 9.8 m/s² is acceptable in calculations." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Acceptable for estimates when the precision of the data does not justify more; use 9.8 or 9.81 for precise answers.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: simplifies arithmetic, only 2% error; other uncertainties (air resistance) are often larger. Arguments against: in precise work 2% matters; g varies with location (9.78-9.83 m/s²). Supported judgement: Acceptable for estimates when the precision of the data does not justify more; use 9.8 or 9.81 for precise answers. items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "velocity–time graph".
items.answer: A graph of velocity against time whose gradient gives acceleration and whose area gives displacement
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a graph of velocity against time whose gradient gives acceleration and whose area gives displacement. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "vector".
items.answer: A quantity that has both magnitude and direction, e.g. displacement, velocity, force, acceleration
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a quantity that has both magnitude and direction, e.g. displacement, velocity, force, acceleration. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Finding the area of a region with straight sloping top as ½ × (sum of parallel sides) × width"?
items.answer: trapezium rule (for v–t graphs)
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of trapezium rule (for v–t graphs).

items.stem: A car travelling at 10 m/s brakes with a deceleration of 4 m/s² for 2 s. Yusuf uses v = u + at and gets v = 10 + 4 × 2 = 18 m/s. Explain the mistake and find the correct velocity.
items.answer: Deceleration means a = −4 m/s²; v = 10 − 4 × 2 = 2 m/s.
items.markingKey: 1 acceleration must be negative because velocity decreases (vector direction opposite to motion); 1 v = 2 m/s.

items.stem: Distinguish between velocity and acceleration.
items.answer: Velocity is the rate of change of displacement (m/s); acceleration is the rate of change of velocity (m/s²).
items.markingKey: Velocity is the rate of change of displacement (m/s); acceleration is the rate of change of velocity (m/s²). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why an object moving in a circle at constant speed has a changing velocity.
items.answer: Velocity is a vector; although the magnitude stays the same, the direction of motion changes continuously, so the velocity changes.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Velocity is a vector; although the magnitude stays the same, the direction of motion changes continuously, so the velocity changes. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why the area under a velocity–time graph gives the distance travelled.
items.answer: Distance = velocity × time; each thin strip of the graph has area velocity × small time interval, so adding all strips (the area) gives total distance.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Distance = velocity × time; each thin strip of the graph has area velocity × small time interval, so adding all strips (the area) gives total distance. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "If a car doubles its speed, its braking distance doubles." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: From v² = u² + 2as, braking distance is proportional to u², so it quadruples.
items.markingKey: From v² = u² + 2as, braking distance is proportional to u², so it quadruples. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: In an investigation into how the height of a ramp affects the average speed of a toy car rolling 1.0 m down it, explain why the same toy car must be kept the same in every trial.
items.answer: mass and friction differ between cars

items.stem:
A cyclist starting from rest recorded her velocity every 2 s on three rides along the same straight road.

Time / s | Velocity / m/s: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
2 | 2.8 | 2.7 | 2.9
4 | 5.5 | 5.7 | 5.6
6 | 8.1 | 8.3 | 8.2
8 | 10.9 | 10.8 | 15.1

Identify the anomalous result. Calculate the mean velocity at 8 s, excluding the anomaly.
items.answer: Anomaly: 15.1 m/s (trial 3 at 8 s); mean = 10.85 m/s

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that self-driving cars will make roads safer.
items.answer: They could reduce human-error crashes significantly, but only with strong testing, regulation and security.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: sensors react faster than humans and do not get tired, drunk or distracted; can measure speeds and distances precisely. items.stem: A sprinter’s velocity–time graph is a curve rising from 0 to 11 m/s over the first 5 s, then flat. Explain how you would estimate the distance covered in the first 5 s from the graph, and explain why simply using ½ × 5 × 11 would give an underestimate.
items.answer: Count squares under the curve and multiply by the distance each square represents (or split into trapezia). The curve rises quickly and lies above the straight line from (0,0) to (5,11), so the triangle area (27.5 m) underestimates the true area.

items.stem: Near a school the speed limit is 13.4 m/s; on the main road it is 20.1 m/s. A driver has a reaction time of 0.8 s and the car decelerates at 7.0 m/s². (a) Calculate the stopping distance at each speed. (b) Show that the braking distance increases by a factor of 2.25 when the speed increases by a factor of 1.5. (c) Use your answers to justify low speed limits near schools.
items.answer: (a) 23.5 m and 44.9 m (b) braking ∝ u², (1.5)² = 2.25 (c) stopping distance is much shorter at low speed, so drivers can stop before hitting a child who steps out
items.markingKey: (a) M1 thinking = u × 0.8; M1 braking = u²/(2 × 7.0); A1 23.5 m; A1 44.9 m. (b) 1 from v² = u² + 2as, s ∝ u². (c) 1 reasoned link to safety/impact speed.
